Just closed The Nine Stitches. Wigman turns failure into a drift‑wood knot—beautiful because it’s stubbornly real. No sugar‑coated “fail forward” mantra, just the uncomfortable truth: maybe failing doesn’t upgrade you; maybe success is learning when not to try. The book refuses easy resilience tips, instead lets the scar tissue of our attempts speak. Those nine stitches aren’t metaphorical; they’re literal proof that things often break before they re‑assemble in a stranger shape. The chapters read like a surgeon’s ledger—methodical, painful, and oddly poetic. Philosophy masquerading as self‑help, refreshing and infuriating in equal measure. Want something deeper than productivity porn? This will irritate you—in the best possible way.

I am curious what this brings up for you.

linkedin:
Just as a piece of timber wears its history in rings—dry spells, bursts of growth—our deepest insights are often sewn straight onto the scars we try to hide.

Each failure is a different chapter than the one we scripted. The flop of a startup taught me more about grit than any trophy ever could. A broken relationship revealed which values were truly mine and which were on loan. Even the most mortifying blunders, when we stare at them without pretense, expose the faulty assumptions we clung to.

The real issue isn’t the scar itself; it’s our refusal to acknowledge it. We sand down our stories until they’re glossy and marketable, stripping away the texture that makes them both interesting and useful to others.

So here’s the brutally honest take: I attempted something hard, it failed, and it reshaped me.

What would happen if we stopped polishing our wounds and started sharing them instead?

Keep this close for the days you need it.
